questions.stem: A 72 year old man has had heartburn for 30 years and has never taken regular treatment. Over 3 months he has had food sticking at the lower end of his sternum, first with bread and now with mashed potato. He has lost 7 kg. His BMI is 31. He has never smoked. Examination is unremarkable.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Adenocarcinoma is the more common type, arising in the lower third from chronic GORD; a squamous cell carcinoma would fit a thin smoker and drinker.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: first with bread and now with mashed potato
steps.x: Long-standing reflux, obesity, progressive dysphagia solids to soft food, weight loss.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Adenocarcinoma of the lower oesophagus.

elim: Dysphagia to solids and liquids from the start, usually in younger patients, without this reflux history.
Can follow reflux but rarely causes 7 kg of weight loss with relentless progression.
Linked to smoking, alcohol and normal BMI, and sits in the middle third.
Gives high dysphagia, regurgitation of old food and halitosis, not lower sternal sticking.

steps.x: **C. Oesophageal adenocarcinoma.** Chronic reflux + obesity + progressive dysphagia + weight loss = adenocarcinoma of the lower third.

questions.stem: A 59 year old woman has a 3 month history of food sticking in the middle of her chest and 6 kg of weight loss. She has smoked 20 cigarettes a day for 40 years and drinks about 50 units of alcohol a week. She has no history of heartburn. Her BMI is 20.
questions.q: Which is the most likely type and site of tumour?
o: Gastrointestinal stromal tumour of the stomach
Small cell carcinoma of the upper third
Squamous cell carcinoma of the middle third
questions.e: Squamous cell carcinoma is strongly linked to tobacco and alcohol, typically in patients of normal BMI, and arises in the middle third; adenocarcinoma is the lower third reflux tumour.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: smoked 20 cigarettes a day for 40 years
steps.x: Heavy smoking and drinking, no reflux, normal BMI, mid-chest dysphagia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Squamous cell carcinoma in the middle third.

elim: Fits chronic reflux, Barrett's and obesity, none of which she has.
Rare, usually presents with bleeding or a mass rather than mid-chest dysphagia.
Benign, slow-growing and does not cause rapid weight loss.
Very rare primary in the oesophagus and does not match the risk profile.

steps.x: **E. Squamous cell carcinoma of the middle third.** Tobacco + alcohol + normal BMI + middle third = squamous cell carcinoma.

questions.stem: A 54 year old woman was diagnosed with achalasia 22 years ago and has had several balloon dilatations. Her swallowing had been stable, but over 2 months it has steadily worsened and she has lost 5 kg. She does not smoke or drink alcohol. Her temperature is 36.7°C and pulse rate 84 bpm.
questions.q: Which malignancy is she at most increased risk of?
questions.e: Stasis in the dilated achalasic oesophagus injures the squamous lining, so achalasia raises the risk of squamous cell carcinoma, not adenocarcinoma.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Long-standing achalasia with a new change in swallowing and weight loss.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Squamous cell carcinoma of the oesophagus.

elim: Linked to H. pylori and atrophic gastritis, not to achalasia.
Linked to smoking; achalasia does not raise its risk.
Arises from Barrett's after chronic reflux; achalasia is the classic squamous risk factor.
Can cause weight loss but has no link with achalasia or dysphagia.

steps.x: **D. Oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma.** Achalasia is a recognised risk factor for oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man has a 2 month history of difficulty swallowing just below his throat and 4 kg of weight loss. For 3 weeks his voice has become hoarse and breathy. He has smoked for 45 years. Flexible nasendoscopy shows a left vocal cord that does not move. There is no mass in the larynx.
questions.q: Where is the tumour most likely to be?
questions.e: A tumour in the upper third can invade the recurrent laryngeal nerve, paralysing the vocal cord and causing hoarseness; lower tumours do not reach the nerve.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: left vocal cord that does not move
steps.x: High dysphagia, hoarse voice, vocal cord palsy with a normal larynx.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: An upper third oesophageal tumour invading the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

elim: Too far from the recurrent laryngeal nerve to cause hoarseness.
A lower tumour causes low dysphagia without vocal cord palsy.
Typical site of adenocarcinoma, far from the nerve's course.
Possible for squamous tumours but the high dysphagia and hoarseness point higher.

steps.x: **E. Upper third of the oesophagus.** Dysphagia + hoarse voice = upper third tumour involving the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man has a 5 month history of progressive dysphagia and has lost 12 kg. He looks thin, with temporal wasting and loose clothing. An OGD 2 weeks ago showed an adenocarcinoma at the gastro-oesophageal junction. His pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
questions.e: Late oesophageal cancer causes cachexia and lymphadenopathy; a hard left supraclavicular node reflects spread via the thoracic duct region.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Late disease: cachexia and a known GOJ tumour.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Cachexia with lymphadenopathy, typically a hard left supraclavicular (Virchow's) node.

elim: Linked to alcohol and diabetes, not to late cancer.
A sign of chronic liver disease, not of nodal spread.
Seen in alcohol excess or Sjögren's, not spread of oesophageal cancer.
Reflects hyperlipidaemia, unrelated to cancer.

steps.x: **B. Hard left supraclavicular lymph node.** Late oesophageal cancer = cachexia + lymphadenopathy, classically the left supraclavicular node.

questions.stem: A 67 year old woman has 2 months of tiredness, pain when she swallows and food coming back up undigested after meals. She has lost 6 kg. She has smoked for 40 years. Her temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Oesophageal cancer can present with odynophagia, regurgitation and anaemia from chronic occult bleeding; candidiasis also causes painful swallowing but not this picture.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Odynophagia, regurgitation, weight loss and a microcytic anaemia from chronic bleeding.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Oesophageal carcinoma.

elim: Long history of dysphagia to liquids and solids; does not cause iron deficiency or rapid weight loss.
Causes iron deficiency but not odynophagia or regurgitation.
A young atopic patient with food bolus impaction, not anaemia and weight loss at 67.
Gives odynophagia in immunosuppressed patients, not regurgitation, anaemia and weight loss.

steps.x: **B. Carcinoma of the oesophagus.** Odynophagia + regurgitation + iron deficiency anaemia + weight loss in an older smoker = oesophageal cancer.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man had an oesophagectomy for adenocarcinoma 14 months ago. He now has 3 weeks of tiredness, yellow eyes and right upper quadrant discomfort. The liver edge is hard and irregular, 4 cm below the costal margin. He drinks 4 units of alcohol a week. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his new findings?
questions.e: Metastasis is a major complication of oesophageal cancer, and the liver is a common site; a hard irregular liver with cholestatic LFTs fits metastases.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Previous oesophageal cancer, jaundice, a hard irregular enlarged liver.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Metastatic spread to the liver.

elim: He drinks only 4 units a week and the liver is hard and irregular, not smooth and tender.
Gives colicky pain with a normal-sized liver, not a craggy liver edge.
Possible on chemotherapy but would not give an irregular hard liver.
Acute illness with a smooth tender liver, not a hard nodular one.

steps.x: **E. Liver metastases.** Previous cancer + craggy hepatomegaly + jaundice = liver metastases.

questions.stem: A 76 year old woman has known oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma and is awaiting treatment. She often coughs during and after meals and food comes back up into her mouth at night. For 2 days she has had a fever and productive cough. Her temperature is 38.4°C, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 92% breathing air. Chest X-ray (see item resources).

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Right lower zone consolidation, the typical site of aspiration.

questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation of these findings?
questions.e: Regurgitation of food above an obstructing tumour leads to aspiration pneumonia, typically in the right lower zone because the right main bronchus is more vertical.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: food comes back up into her mouth at night
steps.x: Regurgitation and coughing with meals, then fever and right lower zone consolidation.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Aspiration pneumonia from regurgitation past the tumour.

elim: Would show volume loss, and the cough with meals points to aspiration.
Gives pleuritic pain and hypoxia with a usually clear X-ray, not fever with consolidation after meals.
Appear as round nodules and do not cause an acute febrile illness.
Usually upper zone, with weeks of night sweats rather than 2 days of fever.

steps.x: **A. Aspiration pneumonia.** Oesophageal obstruction + regurgitation + right lower zone consolidation = aspiration pneumonia.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man with obesity has had reflux for 20 years. He now has progressive dysphagia and 5 kg of weight loss. OGD shows an ulcerated mass in the lower third of the oesophagus just above the gastro-oesophageal junction. Biopsy shows adenocarcinoma. He has never smoked and drinks little alcohol.
questions.q: Which is the most important risk factor for his tumour?
questions.e: Chronic reflux causes Barrett's metaplasia, which progresses through dysplasia to adenocarcinoma; achalasia, alcohol and hot drinks are squamous cell carcinoma risks.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Long reflux history, lower third adenocarcinoma.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Barrett's oesophagus from chronic reflux.

elim: Linked to squamous cell carcinoma, and he drinks little.
Associated with squamous cell carcinoma in some populations.
Linked to oropharyngeal and possibly squamous tumours, not lower third adenocarcinoma.
A risk factor for squamous cell carcinoma, not adenocarcinoma.

steps.x: **B. Barrett's oesophagus.** Chronic GORD causes Barrett's metaplasia, the precursor of lower third adenocarcinoma.

questions.stem: A 74 year old woman has a 2 month history of difficulty swallowing. At first bread and meat stuck, but now she can only manage soup and yoghurt, and this week even water is hard to get down. She has lost 8 kg. She is an ex-smoker. Her pulse rate is 82 bpm and BP 130/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which feature of her history most strongly suggests a malignant cause?
o: Dysphagia progressing from solids to liquids
questions.e: A growing tumour narrows the lumen gradually, so dysphagia progresses from solids to liquids; motility disorders such as achalasia affect both from the start.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: At first bread and meat stuck
now she can only manage soup and yoghurt
steps.x: Relentless progression from solids to liquids with weight loss.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Progressive dysphagia from solids to liquids.

elim: Can occur with any cause of regurgitation, including achalasia.
Common in benign reflux and does not separate cancer from other causes.
Suggest a motility disorder or a ring, not a growing tumour; her symptoms are constant.
Seen in achalasia and pouches as well as cancer.

steps.x: **B. Dysphagia progressing from solids to liquids.** Progressive dysphagia (solids then liquids) + weight loss = malignant stricture until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: A 57 year old man has a 10 week history of food sticking behind his sternum and 6 kg of weight loss. He drinks a bottle of spirits most days and smokes 25 cigarettes a day. His BMI is 22. OGD shows a stricturing mass 27 cm from the incisors, in the middle third of the oesophagus. Biopsies are taken.
questions.q: Which is the most likely histological finding?
questions.e: Squamous cell carcinoma arises in the middle third and is strongly associated with tobacco and alcohol; adenocarcinoma is lower third and reflux-related.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: drinks a bottle of spirits most days
steps.x: Heavy alcohol and tobacco, normal BMI, middle third mass.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Squamous cell carcinoma.

elim: Usually in the lower third in obese patients with reflux and Barrett's.
A submucosal spindle cell tumour, rare in the oesophagus.
Rarely primary in the oesophagus and not linked to smoking and drinking.
Very rare in the oesophagus.

steps.x: **E. Squamous cell carcinoma.** Middle third + smoker + drinker + normal BMI = squamous cell carcinoma.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man has oesophageal adenocarcinoma and is starting neoadjuvant chemotherapy. Over 3 months he has managed only liquids and has lost 14 kg, 18% of his body weight. He has muscle wasting of the arms and legs. His urine dipstick is normal. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his low albumin?
questions.e: Dysphagia limits intake, so malnutrition and cachexia are common complications; a normal dipstick excludes nephrotic syndrome.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: lost 14 kg, 18% of his body weight
steps.x: Months of liquids only, major weight loss, wasting, no proteinuria.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Malnutrition caused by the obstructing tumour.

elim: Would give stigmata of liver disease and a prolonged INR; his LFTs are otherwise normal.
Needs heavy proteinuria, but his urine dipstick is normal.
Rare, with diarrhoea and oedema, and less likely than simple poor intake.
Causes weight loss with a good appetite, tremor and tachycardia, not low albumin.

steps.x: **B. Malnutrition from dysphagia.** Oesophageal cancer causes malnutrition and cachexia; check nutrition before treatment.

questions.stem: A 65 year old man had an oesophagectomy 3 days ago. He has pain from his thoracotomy wound and has been reluctant to cough. He now has a fever and green sputum. His temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 108 bpm, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 91% breathing air. Chest X-ray (see item resources). His drain output is clear.

visual.title: Chest X-ray, day 3
visual.caption: Left lower zone consolidation after thoracotomy.

questions.q: Which is the most likely complication?
questions.e: Postoperative pneumonia is the key complication after oesophagectomy, helped by pain limiting cough; an anastomotic leak usually comes later with cloudy drain fluid.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Day 3 after oesophagectomy, poor cough, purulent sputum, consolidation.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Postoperative pneumonia.

elim: Usually later (day 5 to 7) with sepsis, chest pain and cloudy drain fluid; his drain is clear.
Gives a milky pleural effusion, not fever with green sputum.
Gives sudden breathlessness and pleuritic pain, not productive green sputum and consolidation.
Gives hoarseness and aspiration risk, not fever and consolidation by itself.

steps.x: **C. Postoperative pneumonia.** After oesophagectomy watch for postoperative pneumonia: fever, purulent sputum, consolidation.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man sees his GP with a 6 week history of food sticking in his chest and 4 kg of unintentional weight loss. He has had reflux for many years. Abdominal examination is normal and there are no palpable lymph nodes. His pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 136/84 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Staging CT chest, abdomen and pelvis
questions.e: Urgent (within 2 weeks) upper GI endoscopy with biopsy is first-line and gold standard; barium swallow and empirical PPI delay the diagnosis.

steps.x: It asks for an investigation: think what answers the clinical question right now.
Dysphagia with weight loss is an alarm feature.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Urgent 2-week-wait upper GI endoscopy.

elim: Used for motility disorders such as achalasia, not for suspected cancer.
Shows a stricture but cannot take a biopsy; endoscopy is first-line.
A staging test once cancer is confirmed, not the first investigation.
Delays diagnosis; dysphagia is an alarm symptom needing urgent endoscopy.

steps.x: **A. Direct-access OGD within 2 weeks.** Dysphagia (any age) or weight loss with upper GI symptoms = urgent direct-access OGD within 2 weeks.

questions.stem: A 62 year old woman has an urgent OGD for progressive dysphagia and weight loss. It shows an irregular, friable, ulcerated mass narrowing the lower third of the oesophagus. The endoscope can just pass beyond it. Her haemoglobin is 108 g/L. She is otherwise well and wants to know whether this is cancer.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
o: Biopsy of the mass for histology
questions.e: Diagnosis is confirmed by endoscopy with biopsy; CT, EUS and PET stage the disease once histology is known.

steps.x: It asks for an investigation: think what answers the clinical question right now.

clues: wants to know whether this is cancer
steps.x: A suspicious mass seen at endoscopy needs tissue.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Biopsy at endoscopy for histology.

elim: Stages the tumour but cannot confirm what it is.
Assesses depth of invasion after diagnosis, not the tissue type.
Looks for distant disease; it does not give a histological diagnosis.
A non-specific tumour marker, never diagnostic.

steps.x: **A. Biopsy of the mass for histology.** Endoscopy with biopsy is the gold standard: you need histology before staging or treatment.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man has biopsy-proven adenocarcinoma of the lower oesophagus. He is fit, with a performance status of 0, and is keen on curative treatment. His LFTs are normal and there is no palpable lymphadenopathy. The upper GI multidisciplinary team needs to know whether the disease has spread.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial staging investigation?
questions.e: Staging starts with CT chest, abdomen and pelvis because lymphatic and distant spread can occur early and widely; normal LFTs do not exclude metastases.

steps.x: It asks for an investigation: think what answers the clinical question right now.
Confirmed cancer; now needs staging for distant spread.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis.

elim: Misses chest disease and distant nodes; not adequate for staging.
Only if bone symptoms; not the routine first staging test.
Brain metastases are uncommon; not part of initial staging without symptoms.
Far too insensitive to stage oesophageal cancer.

steps.x: **C. CT chest, abdomen and pelvis.** After biopsy, stage with CT chest, abdomen and pelvis, then EUS for depth.

questions.stem: A 63 year old woman has squamous cell carcinoma of the middle third of the oesophagus. CT chest, abdomen and pelvis shows no distant metastases. Before deciding between surgery alone and treatment before surgery, the surgeons need to know how far the tumour has grown through the oesophageal wall and whether nearby nodes are involved.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
o: Repeat CT chest, abdomen and pelvis
questions.e: Endoscopic ultrasound assesses depth of mural invasion and local nodes, guiding whether neoadjuvant therapy is needed; CT does not resolve the wall layers.

steps.x: It asks for an investigation: think what answers the clinical question right now.

clues: how far the tumour has grown through the oesophageal wall
steps.x: CT has excluded distant spread; the question is local depth (T stage) and nodes.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Endoscopic ultrasound.

elim: Shows the outline of the lumen, not depth of wall invasion.
Already done; CT cannot resolve the layers of the oesophageal wall.
Only needed if airway invasion is suspected.
Looks for peritoneal disease in gastric and junctional tumours, not wall depth.

steps.x: **A. Endoscopic ultrasound.** CT for distant spread, EUS for depth of mural invasion and local nodes.

questions.stem: A 60 year old man had an oesophagectomy for adenocarcinoma after neoadjuvant chemotherapy. Histology showed clear margins. He was discharged home 2 weeks ago, is eating a soft diet and is gaining weight. He asks how he will be checked for recurrence. He has no new symptoms.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate follow-up imaging?
o: MRI of the liver every 2 weeks
questions.e: The notes recommend a follow-up CT at 6 months after discharge following resection; chest X-ray and barium swallow are too insensitive for recurrence.

steps.x: It asks for an investigation: think what answers the clinical question right now.
Post-resection surveillance question.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Follow-up CT at 6 months after discharge.

elim: Not used for surveillance; only for suspected anastomotic problems.
Too insensitive to detect recurrence.
Not a standard follow-up test and far too frequent.
Planned CT follow-up is recommended after resection.

steps.x: **C. CT 6 months after discharge.** After resection, follow up with CT at 6 months after discharge.

questions.stem: A 73 year old woman was sent for a barium swallow by her GP for dysphagia to solids and 5 kg of weight loss. It shows an irregular narrowing with shouldered edges, an 'apple-core' appearance, in the lower oesophagus. She is otherwise well. Her pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: Barium swallow cannot give tissue, so the next step is endoscopy with biopsy, which is both first-line and gold standard.

steps.x: It asks for an investigation: think what answers the clinical question right now.
Malignant-looking stricture on barium, but no tissue yet.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: OGD with biopsy.

elim: Comes after histology confirms cancer.
Assesses depth once the diagnosis is confirmed.
For motility disorders; this is a structural lesion.
Delays diagnosis of a likely cancer.

steps.x: **E. Upper GI endoscopy with biopsy.** Any suspicious stricture must be seen and biopsied: endoscopy with biopsy is gold standard.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man has squamous cell carcinoma of the middle third of the oesophagus. CT shows no metastases. Endoscopic ultrasound shows the tumour extends through the full thickness of the wall with two involved local nodes. He is fit, works full time and has a performance status of 0.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Locally advanced disease is downstaged with neoadjuvant chemotherapy or chemoradiotherapy before oesophagectomy; surgery alone risks leaving tumour behind.

steps.x: It asks for management: decide how sick the patient is and what changes the outcome next.

clues: full thickness of the wall with two involved local nodes
steps.x: Locally advanced, no distant spread, fit patient.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Neoadjuvant treatment, then surgery.

elim: He is fit with curable, non-metastatic disease.
Palliative only, for unresectable disease.
Locally advanced disease needs downstaging first to improve the chance of complete resection.
For unresectable or advanced disease, not curable disease in a fit man.

steps.x: **C. Neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy followed by oesophagectomy.** Locally advanced + no metastases + fit = neoadjuvant chemo(radio)therapy then oesophagectomy.

questions.stem: A 59 year old woman has adenocarcinoma of the lower oesophagus. Endoscopic ultrasound shows it is confined to the submucosa with no involved nodes, and CT chest, abdomen and pelvis shows no metastases. She is fit and has no other medical problems. Her BMI is 27.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
o: High-dose PPI and repeat endoscopy in 6 months
questions.e: Surgical resection (oesophagectomy) is the definitive treatment for early disease; stents and palliative chemotherapy are for advanced disease.

steps.x: It asks for management: decide how sick the patient is and what changes the outcome next.

clues: confined to the submucosa with no involved nodes
steps.x: Early, localised disease in a fit patient.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Surgical resection.

elim: Leaves a curable cancer untreated.
For metastatic or unresectable disease, not early disease.
Feeds the patient but does not treat the cancer.
A palliative measure for unresectable disease.

steps.x: **B. Oesophagectomy.** Early disease in a fit patient = oesophagectomy, the definitive treatment.

questions.stem: An 84 year old man with heart failure has unresectable squamous cell carcinoma of the oesophagus. He can still manage a soft diet. Over 6 weeks he has needed three blood transfusions for oozing from the tumour, seen at endoscopy. He is not fit for chemotherapy. He wants to stay at home.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Regular tranexamic acid and weekly transfusion only
questions.e: Advanced disease is palliative, with an endoscopic stent or radiotherapy; radiotherapy suits a bleeding tumour when swallowing is still adequate.

steps.x: It asks for management: decide how sick the patient is and what changes the outcome next.

clues: can still manage a soft diet
steps.x: Unresectable disease, swallowing adequate, recurrent tumour bleeding.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Palliative radiotherapy.

elim: Relieves dysphagia, but he can swallow a soft diet; the problem is bleeding.
Given before curative surgery, which is not an option here.
Not possible: the tumour is unresectable and he is frail.
Treats the effect, not the bleeding tumour, and ties him to hospital.

steps.x: **D. Palliative radiotherapy.** Unresectable disease is palliated: stent for dysphagia, radiotherapy for bleeding or as an alternative.

questions.stem: A 72 year old woman with known oesophageal adenocarcinoma, awaiting neoadjuvant chemotherapy, attends the emergency department. Since last night she cannot swallow anything, not even her saliva, and is spitting into a bowl. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 116/72 mmHg and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Admit for urgent endoscopic assessment of the obstruction
Discharge with a liquid diet and review in 2 weeks
Increase her proton pump inhibitor dose
questions.e: Severe dysphagia or inability to swallow needs urgent assessment for obstruction (often bolus impaction on a tumour), with IV fluids while nil by mouth.

steps.x: It asks for management: decide how sick the patient is and what changes the outcome next.

clues: cannot swallow anything, not even her saliva
steps.x: Complete dysphagia: an emergency obstruction.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Admit, IV fluids and urgent endoscopic assessment.

elim: Delays treatment of complete obstruction; she cannot even swallow saliva.
She cannot swallow liquids, so she will dehydrate and aspirate.
Does not relieve a mechanical obstruction.
She cannot swallow it, and prokinetics do not open a tumour stricture.

steps.x: **A. Admit for urgent endoscopic assessment of the obstruction.** Total inability to swallow = urgent assessment for obstruction, never outpatient review.

questions.stem: A 63 year old man has adenocarcinoma of the gastro-oesophageal junction. Staging CT shows multiple liver metastases. He can swallow a soft diet, works part-time and has a performance status of 1. He wants treatment that may help him live longer.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Metastatic disease is unresectable, so management is palliative; a fit patient may be offered palliative chemotherapy, with a stent reserved for dysphagia.

steps.x: It asks for management: decide how sick the patient is and what changes the outcome next.
Metastatic, so not curable; but fit and swallowing.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Palliative chemotherapy.

elim: For dysphagia; he swallows a soft diet, so a stent is not yet needed.
Surgery is not curative with liver metastases.
Metastatic disease is unresectable.
Unrelated to oesophageal cancer.

steps.x: **D. Palliative systemic chemotherapy.** Metastatic disease = palliative intent: chemotherapy if fit, stent or radiotherapy for symptoms.

questions.stem: An 88 year old woman with dementia lives in a nursing home. She has a large squamous cell carcinoma of the lower oesophagus with lung metastases. Over 2 weeks she has stopped managing anything but sips of water and is distressed at mealtimes. Her family want her to be comfortable and eat if possible.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate intervention to relieve her dysphagia quickly?
questions.e: An endoscopic self-expanding metal stent gives rapid palliation of dysphagia in unresectable disease; radiotherapy relieves dysphagia more slowly.

steps.x: It asks for management: decide how sick the patient is and what changes the outcome next.
Metastatic disease, frail, near-total dysphagia, goal is comfort.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: An endoscopic stent.

elim: Part of curative treatment, which is not appropriate.
Not possible with metastases and frailty.
Too toxic for her and slow to help swallowing.
Invasive, needs central access and does not let her eat.

steps.x: **D. Self-expanding metal stent.** Fastest relief of malignant dysphagia in palliative care = endoscopic stent.

questions.stem: A 56 year old man with locally advanced adenocarcinoma of the lower oesophagus has completed neoadjuvant chemotherapy. Repeat CT shows the tumour has shrunk with no new metastases. He has kept his weight stable and his performance status is 0. His surgeon reviews him in clinic.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.e: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy downstages the tumour so that oesophagectomy, the definitive treatment, can achieve complete resection.

steps.x: It asks for management: decide how sick the patient is and what changes the outcome next.
Downstaged by neoadjuvant therapy, still no metastases, fit.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Proceed to surgical resection.

elim: That is palliative; he has responded and is now resectable.
Not appropriate for curable disease.
For palliation of unresectable disease.
Leaves the residual tumour to regrow.

steps.x: **A. Oesophagectomy.** Neoadjuvant therapy is followed by oesophagectomy, the definitive treatment.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man has had reflux for 15 years. Surveillance biopsies of his distal oesophagus over 8 years first showed columnar epithelium with goblet cells, then low-grade and later high-grade dysplasia. He has now developed an invasive tumour at the same site. He asks how this happened.

steps.x: **E. Metaplasia, then dysplasia, then carcinoma.** Barrett's: metaplasia then dysplasia then adenocarcinoma.

questions.stem: A 47 year old woman has had heartburn and bile regurgitation for many years. An OGD shows salmon-pink mucosa extending 4 cm above the gastro-oesophageal junction. questions.stem: A 60 year old man has squamous cell carcinoma of the oesophagus. He has smoked 30 cigarettes a day since he was 16 and drinks 70 units of alcohol a week. o: Smoking causes acid reflux which leads to squamous cancer
Tobacco and alcohol act synergistically on the squamous epithelium
Tobacco and alcohol each add a small independent risk
questions.e: Squamous cell carcinoma results from direct carcinogenic injury to the native squamous epithelium, and tobacco and alcohol act synergistically.

questions.stem: A 75 year old man has a stricturing oesophageal adenocarcinoma. Three months ago steak stuck, a month ago bread stuck, and now he can only swallow thickened fluids. Gradual circumferential narrowing of the lumen by tumour
Loss of inhibitory neurons in the myenteric plexus
questions.e: Dysphagia progresses from solids to liquids because the tumour gradually narrows the lumen as it grows circumferentially; achalasia is a motility problem affecting both from the start.
